x: ← Project Scroll About About Project Scroll Project Scroll is independent historical research: a history hunt anyone can play, a research desk anyone can hire, and a studio for digital imaging, design, photography, 3D LiDAR, animation and video. All of it runs on one rule. Every clue is true, and every answer is in the record. Who we are Project Scroll is run by an independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, and who trained in visual communications. The research behind those books is the same research we offer you: old certificates, deeds, surveys, county histories and newspapers, read line by line and compared until they agree, or until we can say exactly why they don’t. What we offer Professional research. Lost ancestors, family histories and registers, family legends tested against the record, forgotten places, maps and land surveys, heirlooms, lodges and old societies, historical research for authors, films and local groups, and a second pair of eyes on anything you mean to publish. Research services . Imaging, design and video. Digital imaging of photographs, documents, maps and heirlooms; imaging analysis of faded ink, damaged pages and the details in old photographs; image creation and restoration; graphic design for family books, charts, covers and keepsakes; photography; and video production, from family-history films to recorded interviews. 3D and living documents. Landscapes modelled in three dimensions from public LiDAR elevation surveys, 3D animations and fly-throughs, every reconstruction labelled as one, and living documents: research papers, timelines and family records that keep growing as new evidence turns up, with every change dated. The studio . Every commission starts with an honest first read: what can be done, and what it will take, before you commit to anything. What we believe The record decides. Not the family tree online, not the story everybody tells, not what we hoped to find. Every statement is marked. You can always see whether a fact comes from a document, a book, a family story or our own reading. How we mark the evidence . Gaps are shown, not filled. An honest “not yet known” is worth more than a confident guess. Corrections are welcome. If you know better, tell us. The record is bigger than any one of us. Places and people are respected. The hunt never asks anyone to dig, to disturb a grave or a mound, or to go looking for anyone’s home. Where it started Project Scroll began in Cassopolis, Michigan, with a few questions the county history couldn’t answer. It doesn’t stop there. The hunt and the desk now take on questions from anywhere the records reach. Play the hunt Research services Imaging, design and video Get in touch

← Research services Research services Family histories, built to be checked Most family trees are copied from other family trees. Ours are built from the records themselves: every name, date and place marked with where it came from, every gap shown honestly, and every family story kept exactly as it was told, beside the evidence that tests it. What we make Looking down A family register Every descendant of one couple, generation by generation, each person given a number, so that a reader can follow any branch from the first settlers to the present day. The form genealogists have trusted for 150 years. Looking back An ancestral monograph Your ancestors, back as far as the records honestly go, on a single chart. Where a line stops, it says whose parents are wanting, so you can see at a glance what is known, what is not, and where to look next. The whole story A family history Every line written up as a story, with the evidence beneath it: maps, records, a list of every source, an index of names and places, and the open questions set out for the next person to take up. A specimen monograph Here is how an ancestral monograph works, using an invented family. Tap anyone to see what we know about them, and how we know it. Specimen. The names are invented; the method is real. Tap a name in the chart. “Clara ?” A question mark means the marriage is recorded but her own surname is not. Women are usually recorded under their husbands’ names, which is not the same as being born with them. “Wanting” An empty box beside a known person is a real gap: someone we could find tomorrow. The boxes beyond the edge of the chart, behind Clara’s missing parents, are not gaps at all. There is nothing to look for there until her parents are found. The warning sign. When two records cannot both be true, the chart flags the joint and leaves it in. Never solve a problem by deleting the evidence. How a register reads 1. AUGUST¹ BRANDT was born about 1862 Inference and died in 1931 Document . He married WILHELMINA KRAUSE , born in 1866 Document . Children of August and Wilhelmina: + 2 i. OTTO² , born 1890; married CLARA ? ii. Emma, born 1893; died 1894, aged one. The small raised number is the generation. The plus sign means Otto’s own family is carried forward under his number, 2, so a reader can follow his line on down without losing the thread. (The same invented family as the chart above.) Lessons from our own desk Real lessons, every one learned the hard way on a family history built at this desk. A woman dies under her married name. For years a death certificate went unfound because everyone searched for her under her maiden name. It was filed under her husband’s. Search the unusual name. A rare surname finds the family and almost nobody else. A common one needs a place and a date beside it, or it finds thousands. A strong lead in the right county is still not a parent. A well-documented man of the right name, in the right place, at the right time, turned out to be no relation at all. The answer was in a different family. An abstract is not a record. A published summary of a colonial will gave two witnesses’ names and a probate date. The court’s own record disagreed on both. “About” must stay “about”. A birth year worked out from an age at death was printed beside real dates, and soon looked like one. Estimates are marked as estimates, always. The best finds are in free books nobody opened. Lines written off as dead ends turned out to be answered in county histories and family genealogies that had been free online for years. Dead ends don’t get searched. Starting your family’s history Tell us who. One couple to work down from, or one person to work back from. Names, places, rough dates. Send what the family has. Bible pages, letters, photographs, obituaries, old trees. We read every one, and we keep every family story exactly as it was told. Agree on the shape. ← Project Scroll From the desk The glossary The words old records use, and the words we use about them, in plain English. Find a word Abstract A summary of a document, such as a deed or will, giving its main points. Useful for finding the original, but not the record itself: abstracts drop words and sometimes get names and dates wrong. Administrator The person a court appoints to settle the estate of someone who died without a will. Compare executor. Ahnentafel German for “ancestor table.” A numbering system for a pedigree: the subject is 1, a person’s father is double their number and their mother double plus one. So 2 is the father, 3 the mother, 4 the father’s father. Census A count of the population. The United States has taken one every ten years since 1790; from 1850 it names every free person in the household (enslaved people were counted on separate schedules, usually without names, until 1870). Most of the 1890 census was destroyed after a fire in 1921. Each census is opened to the public 72 years after it was taken. Consort A husband or wife. Often seen on old gravestones: “Mary, consort of John Smith.” County history The big county histories printed from the 1870s to the 1910s. Many biographies in them were paid for by the people they describe, so they tend to be accurate on names and dates and generous on everything else. Deed The written record of land changing hands, copied into the county’s deed books. Deeds often name wives, heirs and neighbors, and sometimes say where a seller had moved to. Double dating Dates such as “10 February 1731/2.” Before 1752, England and its colonies began the new year on 25 March, so January to March dates were often written with both years. Et ux. Latin, “and wife,” in deeds and court records: “John Smith et ux.” means John and his wife. Executor The person named in a will to carry it out. Compare administrator. Field notes A surveyor’s notebook from the original land survey, recording every line walked: the trees, streams, soil and sometimes the people met along the way. General Land Office The federal office that surveyed and sold public land, from 1812 until it became part of the Bureau of Land Management in 1946. Its plats, field notes and patents are online free. Informant The person who answered the questions on a certificate. On a death certificate the dead person was never the informant, so everything on it is someone else’s memory. Instant and ultimo Old newspaper shorthand: “the 4th inst.” means the 4th of this month; “the 20th ult.” the 20th of last month. Intestate Having died without a will. The court then appoints an administrator and divides the estate by law. Land patent The first transfer of a piece of land from the government to a private owner. Maiden name A woman’s surname before marriage. Most records name married women only by their husbands’ surnames, which is why a woman’s own family is the commonest gap in any tree. mtDNA and Y-DNA Two DNA tests that follow one line each: mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child down the all-female line; Y-DNA passes from father to son down the all-male line. Naturalization The process of becoming a citizen. Older files often have two parts: a declaration of intention (“first papers”) and, years later, a petition. Later ones can name the town of birth and the ship. Pedigree collapse When the same ancestor appears more than once in a family tree because cousins married. It means fewer separate ancestors than the arithmetic of doubling would suggest. Plat A surveyor’s drawing of land divided into lots or parcels, such as a town plan or a subdivision. Probate The court process that settles a dead person’s estate. A probate file can hold the will, an inventory of belongings, and the names of every heir. Register system The standard way of numbering a family register, used by American genealogists since the 1800s. t: How to read a death certificate
x: ← Project Scroll A guide from the desk How to read a death certificate A death certificate is two records in one. The doctor wrote down the death, at the time. Someone else, the informant, answered questions about a whole life, on the hardest day. Tap any numbered box to see who filled it in, and how far to trust it. Box 11 Informant Filled in by: How far to trust it: Every box, in order The rule of thumb The top half (boxes 3 to 10) is memory : what the informant believed about a life. The bottom half (boxes 12 to 16) is the event : written by people who were there that week. When the two halves disagree with other records, trust the bottom half first, and weigh the top half by who the informant was. Michigan’s certificates from 1897 to 1952 are free to view at the Archives of Michigan . Elsewhere, try FamilySearch or your state archives. See it in a real case Hunter’s worksheet (PDF)

← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk Reading the old hand The writing in old records is not hard once you know a dozen tricks the clerks used. Here they are, with a short quiz at the end. The clerks’ tricks ſ The long s Looks like an f without the full crossbar. Used at the start or middle of a word until about 1800: “Congreſs”, “ſon”, “Miſsiſsippi”. Read it as an ordinary s. ye “Ye” means “the” The y stands for an old letter, thorn (þ), pronounced “th”. “Ye olde inn” was always read “the old inn”. Likewise “yt” = that, “ym” = them. Wm · Jno · Chas Shortened first names Clerks raised the last letters: Wm = William, Jno = John (not Jonathan), Chas = Charles, Thos = Thomas, Jas = James, Geo = George, Saml = Samuel, Benj = Benjamin. inst. · ult. · prox. Which month? “The 4th inst.” = the 4th of this month. “The 20th ult.” = the 20th of last month. “The 2nd prox.” = the 2nd of next month. Check the date of the letter or newspaper to know which month. do. Ditto “do.” under an entry means “the same as above”. Census takers and clerks used it for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. &c. Et cetera The ampersand plus c: “and so on”. Often written as a looped sign that can look like a letter. 1745/6 Double dates Before 1752 in England and its colonies, the new year began on 25 March. A date between January and March is often written with both years. Use the later one for today’s calendar. relict · consort On gravestones “Relict of John Smith” = his widow (she outlived him). “Consort of” = his wife, who died while he was living. dec’d · Esq. In deeds and wills dec’d = deceased. Esq. = Esquire, a courtesy for a lawyer or a man of standing, not a title of nobility. 71y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age at death in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death with the age calculator . Test yourself Six questions. A letter dated 10 June says “your note of the 28th ult.” When was the note written? “ult.” means last month: 28 May. In a 1790 newspaper you read “Congreſs”. What does it say? That f-like letter is the long s. A census line reads “Jno Smith” and below it “do. do.” What is the second person’s name? Jno is John, and do. repeats the line above. A gravestone reads “Mary, relict of Amos Hale.” What does it tell you? A relict outlived her husband. A baptism is dated “12 February 1734/5”. Which year is it on today’s calendar? Use the later year for January to March dates before 1752. “Ye Olde Tavern” was read aloud as… The y stands for the old letter thorn, “th”. Back to the toolkit How to read a death certificate

Part IV Bring us your mystery Some questions have waited a hundred years for someone to look properly. If the answer was ever written down, we will look for it, and tell you honestly what we find. And when what you have is a faded photograph, a fragile page or a story worth showing, the studio can image it, restore it, design it, model it in 3D or film it. Cases from our desk A pioneer whose death certificate and his son’s can’t agree on his middle initial. A lake the 1882 county history said was fed by a river running underground from Lake Superior. A small-town doctor’s 1849 trek to the California gold fields, and a typescript of it listed in a museum’s collection, still waiting to be read for the hunt. Two certificates Michigan death certificates, 1912 and 1935, Archives of Michigan. The father’s own certificate gives no middle initial; his son’s, filled in twenty-three years later, gives him one. The underground river History of Cass County, Michigan (1882): “It is supposed by many people” that the lake is a surface spot of a great subterranean stream from Lake Superior. Free on archive.org. The gold-rush doctor Portrait and Biographical Record of Berrien and Cass Counties, Michigan (1893), quoting his 1892 obituary; and the Oregon-California Trails Association’s trail-diary bibliography, which lists his “Journey to California” typescript. Real cases, every one begun as a single question. All of them are still open, and when one is answered we will say so. Now we’re taking on yours. What we research A lost ancestor Census rolls, death certificates, deeds, wills, church books and old newspapers, compared line by line. When the records disagree, we work out who was remembering, and when. Who said it first A family story, a famous quote or a local legend, traced back to the first time it was printed. Who wrote it down? Were they there? Who told them? What changed each time it was retold? A forgotten place A vanished mill, a schoolhouse, a cabin or a whole village, found again on old plat maps, surveyors’ field notes and county atlases. A local legend worth testing Giant bones, underground rivers, buried treasure. We read the story against the records and tell you which parts hold up and which don’t. An heirloom no one can explain An old photograph, a lodge badge, a deed, a letter or a piece of jewelry, traced through the people who owned it. Part V How we work Five promises we keep on every case and commission, whether it takes an afternoon or a season. Every claim comes with its source. You’ll know exactly where each fact came from, so you can check it yourself. Disagreements are clues, not failures. When two records argue, we show you both and explain why. Open questions stay open. If something might be true but can’t be proven yet, we say so, and we keep looking instead of throwing it away. No guarantees, just the record. Some questions have answers on paper and some don’t. We’ll tell you up front which kind yours looks like. We research the past. No locating living people, no legal or title opinions, no appraisals. No digging, no trespassing, and care with every family’s story. State of Michigan, record of deaths, Allegan County. We read the page itself, not someone’s summary of it. What you get A written report in plain English: what we found, where we found it, what is still open, and where to look next. Where the old books and maps are free online, we include the links so you can turn the pages yourself. For studio work, you get the finished images, design files or film, and your originals back as you sent them. See a sample report .

Part VI How we mark the evidence Not every source is worth the same. A death certificate filed the week a man died is not a story his grandson told sixty years later, and neither of them is our own opinion. So in our longer research reports, every statement carries one of nine marks, strongest first. You can see at a glance what the record says, and what we are arguing from it. What the record says What we argue from it Strongest Weakest What the record says Document Made at the time, by someone whose job was to write it down: a death certificate, a deed, a census page, a survey, a map. Example: a 1912 Michigan death certificate. Period print Printed at or near the time: a newspaper notice, an obituary, a book of the day. Example: a doctor’s obituary printed the year he died. County history The big county histories of the 1870s to the 1910s. Rich and indispensable, but often written decades later from what families remembered, and rarely checked. Example: the 1882 History of Cass County. Compiled A later hand gathering earlier records: an index, a bibliography, a transcription, a modern summary. Good for finding things; we go back to the original whenever it survives. Example: a trail-diary bibliography that lists an unpublished typescript. Tradition What a family or a community says, passed down by word of mouth. Worth recording exactly as told, and worth testing. Example: “Grandpa always said he came over on the last boat before the war.” Field What we saw or measured ourselves, at first hand, dated, from public ground or with permission. Example: a dated photograph of a marker on a public roadside. What we argue from it Inference A step that follows directly from the records. Example: one certificate was filed a month after he died, the other twenty-three years later, so the first informant was closer to the event. Reading Our interpretation of what the records point to. Always labeled, always open to correction. Example: “In 1935, someone gave the father his son’s initial.” Hypothesis An idea worth testing that the records don’t yet support. We say what would prove or disprove it. Example: he never used a middle initial at all; his obituary and gravestone would tell. Marks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — the last three marks are our own argument, offered for correction How it looks in a report A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. His death certificate gives no middle initial Document . A county history adds “Senior” to his name County history . His son’s death certificate, filled in twenty-three years later, gives the father a middle initial: the son’s own Document . The first informant was closer to the event Inference . Father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . Or he never used a middle initial at all, which his obituary would show Hypothesis . Tap a mark to see what it means. From our case “ One Letter, Two Certificates .” Every report you receive from us is marked the same way. Weigh the evidence Add records to each side and watch the scale. Records are weighed, not counted: one good document can outweigh a pile of family stories. Side A Side B The scale is level. Add a record to either side. The weights are a rule of thumb, not a formula: a late or careless document can still be wrong, and a detailed tradition can still be right. Try marking these yourself Pick the mark you would give each one. A notice in the local paper, the week after he died. Period print. It was printed at the time, but by a newspaper, not by an office whose job was to record the death. “Great-aunt Ruth always said the family came from Ohio.” Tradition. Write it down exactly as she said it, then go and test it. A website listing every burial in a cemetery, typed up by volunteers. Compiled. A later hand gathered it. Wonderful for finding a name; then find the original burial record or the stone

Part VII From the field notes The first lesson from the desk: what to do when two old records tell you two different things. Ask who gave the information, and when. Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. Write down both versions and where each came from. Never quietly “fix” one. Call it settled only when the evidence settles it. Until then, it’s an open question. ← Research services Mysteries in the family Is the family story true? Every family has a story that has been told so often nobody questions it. Some are true. Some are half-true. Some began as a guess a hundred years ago. The records can usually tell which. Test a family legend Choose the story your family tells. Pick a story above to see what the records usually say about it, and how we would test yours. Tradition What families say. An inspector couldn’t spell it, so he wrote down something easier, and that became the family name. Document What the records usually show. Ellis Island inspectors did not write names down; they checked arrivals against passenger lists made at the port of departure. Names did change, often, but usually years later and by the family itself: at naturalization, at work, at school, or simply over time. How we test it Find the passenger list: it shows the name as written where the journey began. Find the naturalization papers, which often record both the old name and the new one. Follow the name census by census to see when the new spelling first appears. Reading The change almost always happened. Ellis Island almost never did it. Tradition What families say. A lord, a king, a governor or a famous founder sits at the top of the tree. Document What the records usually show. Some of these are true. Many began as a name match: someone of the right surname, in roughly the right place, adopted into the tree a century ago and copied forward until it looked like fact. How we test it Test the line one link at a time, starting with the most recent. Every parent–child joint needs its own record. Find who first printed the claim, and what they cited. Check the famous person’s documented children against the one the family claims. Reading Worth testing. Usually the line breaks at one particular joint, and finding it is a story in itself. Tradition What families say. A grandmother or great-grandmother was a Native princess, often said to be Cherokee. Document What the records usually show. The Cherokee Nation did not have princesses, and the story is so widespread that historians treat it as a family-legend pattern of its own. Some families do have Native ancestry, and the records that show it are specific: tribal rolls, agency censuses and treaty and allotment papers. How we test it Name the ancestor and place her in a census, with the people around her. Search the tribal rolls of the place and period (for the Cherokee: the Dawes and Guion Miller rolls, and the earlier rolls before them). A DNA test cannot show tribal membership; only the records and the nation itself can. Reading The princess is almost never real. The ancestor sometimes is, and deserves to be found properly. Tradition What families say. Three brothers arrived on one ship: one went north, one went south and one went west. Document What the records usually show. It is one of the most common stories in American family lore. Sometimes there were three brothers. Often there were three men of the same surname who were not related at all, later joined together to explain why the name turns up in different places. How we test it Find each man separately in the passenger lists, censuses and land records. Look for a document that names them as brothers: a will, a deed, a probate file. For male lines, a Y-DNA test can say whether their descendants share a father at all. Reading Often half-true: the men were real; the brotherhood is the part to test. Tradition What families say. Everything was lost in the fire, so there is no point looking. Document What the records usually show. Courthouses did burn, and records were lost. But deeds were often re-recorded afterward by the owners, and copies survive in state archives, churches, newspapers, tax rolls, military files and the records of neighboring counties. How we test it Find out exactly which years and which books were lost: it is rarely everything. Look for deeds re-recorded after the fire. Go around it: st

Here a son with the same name does turn up, so the label fits, but always check. Disagreement is a clue, not a failure. Every mismatch tells you who was remembering, and when. ← Project Scroll The hunter’s toolkit Tools for reading the record Four small tools we use at the desk every day. They run entirely in your browser: nothing you type or load here is sent anywhere. Faded-ink enhancer Load a photo of an old letter, deed, certificate or page. Slide until the writing stands out, then save the clearer copy. Your photo never leaves your device. Choose a photo No photo chosen. Brightness Contrast Lift faded ink Sharpen Black and white Invert (light writing on dark) Age at death → birth date Old certificates and gravestones often give age to the day: “aged 71 years, 4 months, 12 days.” Count back from the date of death and you have a birth date to test against everything else. Date of death Years Months Days Remember: the informant gave that age, so it is a clue to test, not a proof. Stones carved years later can be off too. Soundex finder The indexes to the 1880 to 1930 censuses, made in the 1930s and 1940s, were filed by Soundex, a code that groups surnames that sound alike. Type a surname to get its code and spellings worth searching. Surname Cousin calculator Start from the ancestor two people share. Say how each one descends from that ancestor, and the calculator names the relationship. Cipher wheel The simplest secret writing of all: every letter slides the same number of places along the alphabet. Turn the wheel until the line makes sense.
